title: Palo Alto Networks Certified Cybersecurity Entry-level Technician (PCCET)

nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals (CLF-C02 / AZ-900 / CCNA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cloud fundamentals questions appear on almost every entry-level certification. They test your ability to map a business requirement to the correct service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), understand the provider vs customer responsibility split, and compare on-premises capex to cloud opex — all before any technical deep-dive.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — who manages what in each model?
flashcards.back: IaaS (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine): provider manages hardware + hypervisor; you manage OS, runtime, app, data. PaaS (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine): provider adds OS + runtime; you manage app + data. SaaS (Office 365, Salesforce): provider manages everything; you manage user config and data. As you move up the stack you trade control for speed.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — where is the exact dividing line?
flashcards.back: The provider is always responsible for security OF the cloud (physical data centers, networking fabric, hypervisor, managed service software). The customer is always responsible for security IN the cloud (data classification, IAM configuration, OS patching on IaaS VMs, application code). The dividing line shifts up the stack for PaaS and SaaS — the more managed the service, the more the provider owns.

flashcards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones — what is each?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic cluster of data centers (e.g., us-east-1, West Europe). An AZ is one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power, cooling, and networking. AZs in a region are close enough for low-latency synchronous replication but far enough apart that a fire/flood in one doesn't hit another. Spread workloads across at least 2 AZs for high availability.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud shift the spending model?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): large upfront purchase of hardware that you then depreciate over years; on-premises servers. Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing pay-as-you-go cost; cloud compute bills. Cloud converts infra from capex to opex — no hardware procurement lead times, costs scale with actual usage, easier to budget for a startup or to kill a failed project without a sunk-cost legacy.

questions.q: A security architect is describing the goals of an organization's information-security program to a new board member. They want a single, widely accepted model that names the three foundational properties every security control ultimately protects. Which model should they cite?
choices: The CIA triad — Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
The AAA framework — Authentication, Authorization, Accounting.
The Parkerian hexad — Utility, Possession, Authenticity, and the three CIA properties.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework core functions — Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
questions.explanation: The CIA triad — Confidentiality (only authorised parties can read the data), Integrity (data is not altered in transit or at rest), and Availability (systems and data are accessible when needed) — is the canonical model of the three foundational security properties. AAA is an access-control framework for identity workflows, not a description of what security protects. The Parkerian hexad extends CIA with three extra properties but is far less commonly cited in board-level briefings. The NIST CSF describes operational functions of a security program, not the properties every control aims to preserve.

questions.q: An analyst is inventorying every internet-exposed asset the company owns: public IP addresses, cloud storage buckets, mobile apps, SaaS admin portals, remote-worker VPN gateways, and unmanaged shadow-IT services. What term best describes the total set of these exposures that an external attacker could probe?
choices: The threat model.
The attack surface.
The blast radius.
The kill chain.
questions.explanation: An attack surface is the sum of all points (network, application, cloud, human) where an unauthorised party can attempt to enter, extract data from, or affect an environment. A threat model is the structured analysis of what could go wrong for a given asset and who might cause it — a process, not the exposure itself. Blast radius is the scope of damage after a compromise happens. The kill chain describes the sequence of attacker actions during an intrusion, not the exposure being enumerated.

questions.q: A finance clerk receives an email that looks like it comes from their CFO, urgently asking them to wire funds to a new supplier. The message uses the CFO's real name, mentions a real ongoing acquisition, and is addressed only to that clerk. Which social-engineering technique is being described?
choices: Spear phishing — a targeted message crafted for a specific individual using researched context.
Generic phishing broadcast to any recipient without personalisation.
Smishing — a phishing message delivered by SMS.
Vishing — a phishing attempt delivered by voice call.
questions.explanation: Spear phishing is a phishing attack aimed at a specific individual and personalised with details the attacker has researched (job title, ongoing projects, colleagues' names) to raise credibility. Generic phishing is broadcast to large lists and lacks such personalisation. Smishing and vishing describe the delivery channel (SMS and voice, respectively) rather than the targeting pattern. When the target is a senior executive rather than a mid-level employee, the term used is whaling, but the scenario here targets the clerk, not the CFO.

questions.q: A CIO is comparing a legacy port-based stateful firewall with a next-generation firewall (NGFW). Which capability is characteristic of an NGFW but NOT provided by a traditional stateful firewall?
choices: Tracking the state of TCP connections in a session table.
Blocking or allowing traffic based on source/destination IP and TCP/UDP port.
Identifying the application inside a session regardless of port and enforcing per-application policy.
Performing basic NAT translations for outbound traffic.
questions.explanation: The defining capability of a next-generation firewall is application awareness — the firewall identifies the actual application riding a session (for example App-ID recognising a Skype call or SSH-over-443) independent of the TCP/UDP port used, and enforces policy on that identity. Stateful connection tracking, port/IP filtering, and NAT are baseline features of any modern stateful firewall and predate NGFWs. NGFWs also typically add integrated IPS, TLS decryption, URL filtering, and user identification, but application awareness is the core differentiator called out on the PCCET blueprint.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A security lead is briefing an executive on Zero Trust and needs to state the single guiding principle in one sentence. Which statement most accurately captures Zero Trust?
flashcards.back: Zero Trust removes the notion of an implicitly trusted internal network. Every access request — user, device, workload, API — is authenticated, authorised, and continuously validated based on identity, device posture, and context, and it is granted only the least privilege needed. The other options describe classic perimeter-only security models that Zero Trust was created to replace, or the exact anti-pattern (broad standing privilege) it seeks to eliminate.

flashcards.front: A network engineer is designing a segmentation strategy for a data centre. They want to place workloads that host regulated data into their own zone so that policy between zones is enforced by the firewall. Which control best implements this design?
flashcards.back: Zone-based segmentation on an NGFW places workloads with similar trust or compliance requirements into named zones and enforces inter-zone policy at the firewall. This is the standard implementation of network segmentation and micro-segmentation strategies aimed at containing lateral movement. A flat VLAN eliminates segmentation entirely. Relying only on host firewalls provides no centralised control and no independent enforcement plane. Disabling logging directly undermines the visibility segmentation is meant to provide.

flashcards.front: An engineer is mapping responsibilities for a workload running on a cloud provider's Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) offering. Under the standard cloud shared-responsibility model, which of the following is the CUSTOMER responsible for on IaaS?
flashcards.back: On IaaS, the provider is responsible for security OF the cloud — physical facilities, hypervisor, networking hardware, power, and cooling. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud, which on IaaS includes the guest OS (patching, hardening), application code, identity and access management, network/security-group configuration, and data protection. The other options belong squarely to the provider's side of the boundary. On PaaS the boundary moves higher (provider also covers OS/runtime); on SaaS higher still (customer mostly retains data, identity, and configuration responsibilities).

flashcards.front: A developer explains the difference between a container and a virtual machine to a junior colleague. Which statement about containers is correct?
flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel through OS-level virtualisation (namespaces, cgroups) and package only the application binary and its dependencies. That is what makes them faster to start and much lighter than VMs, which each carry a full guest OS and run on a hypervisor. Orchestrators such as Kubernetes are purpose-built to run containers at scale. Immutability of an image does not eliminate supply-chain risk — vulnerable or malicious base images and dependencies remain a common attack path, which is why image scanning is a core cloud-security control.

questions.q: A security lead is briefing an executive on Zero Trust and needs to state the single guiding principle in one sentence. Which statement most accurately captures Zero Trust?
choices: Trust everything inside the corporate LAN; distrust everything on the internet.
Rely on a hardened perimeter firewall so that internal east-west traffic can flow without inspection.
Grant broad administrator rights to trusted employees so they can move freely across systems.
Never trust and always verify — authenticate and authorise every user, device, and workload for every request, regardless of network location.
questions.explanation: Zero Trust removes the notion of an implicitly trusted internal network. Every access request — user, device, workload, API — is authenticated, authorised, and continuously validated based on identity, device posture, and context, and it is granted only the least privilege needed. The other options describe classic perimeter-only security models that Zero Trust was created to replace, or the exact anti-pattern (broad standing privilege) it seeks to eliminate.

questions.q: A network engineer is designing a segmentation strategy for a data centre. They want to place workloads that host regulated data into their own zone so that policy between zones is enforced by the firewall. Which control best implements this design?
choices: Deploying a single flat VLAN so all servers can reach each other with minimum latency.
Creating separate network zones on the NGFW (for example `trust`, `dmz`, `pci`) and writing security policies that reference those zones.
Allowing the workloads to keep their public IPs and relying on host-based firewalls only.
Disabling logging on internal traffic to reduce noise in the SIEM.
questions.explanation: Zone-based segmentation on an NGFW places workloads with similar trust or compliance requirements into named zones and enforces inter-zone policy at the firewall. This is the standard implementation of network segmentation and micro-segmentation strategies aimed at containing lateral movement. A flat VLAN eliminates segmentation entirely. Relying only on host firewalls provides no centralised control and no independent enforcement plane. Disabling logging directly undermines the visibility segmentation is meant to provide.

questions.q: An engineer is mapping responsibilities for a workload running on a cloud provider's Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) offering. Under the standard cloud shared-responsibility model, which of the following is the CUSTOMER responsible for on IaaS?
choices: Guest operating-system patching, application code, IAM configuration, and data.
Physical security of the data centre and hypervisor patching.
The underlying storage-array firmware and network switch fabric.
The health of the region's power and cooling.
questions.explanation: On IaaS, the provider is responsible for security OF the cloud — physical facilities, hypervisor, networking hardware, power, and cooling. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud, which on IaaS includes the guest OS (patching, hardening), application code, identity and access management, network/security-group configuration, and data protection. The other options belong squarely to the provider's side of the boundary. On PaaS the boundary moves higher (provider also covers OS/runtime); on SaaS higher still (customer mostly retains data, identity, and configuration responsibilities).

questions.q: A developer explains the difference between a container and a virtual machine to a junior colleague. Which statement about containers is correct?
choices: Each container runs a full guest operating system on top of a hypervisor.
Containers require dedicated physical hardware and cannot be orchestrated at scale.
Containers eliminate all software-supply-chain risk because their images are immutable.
Containers share the host operating-system kernel and package only the application plus its dependencies, making them lighter than VMs.
questions.explanation: Containers share the host kernel through OS-level virtualisation (namespaces, cgroups) and package only the application binary and its dependencies. That is what makes them faster to start and much lighter than VMs, which each carry a full guest OS and run on a hypervisor. Orchestrators such as Kubernetes are purpose-built to run containers at scale. Immutability of an image does not eliminate supply-chain risk — vulnerable or malicious base images and dependencies remain a common attack path, which is why image scanning is a core cloud-security control.

nodes.title: Automation and IaC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

questions.q: A CISO wants a single service that identifies risky SaaS use, enforces DLP on sanctioned SaaS apps, and blocks access to unsanctioned ones. Which technology should they evaluate first?
choices: A traditional stateful firewall at the internet edge.
A hardware VPN concentrator.
A Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB).
A traditional signature-based antivirus product on each endpoint.
questions.explanation: A Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) sits between users and SaaS applications, discovers sanctioned and unsanctioned SaaS use (shadow IT), enforces DLP, applies threat protection, and can control access based on user, device, and risk. Stateful firewalls do not have SaaS-app awareness or DLP for cloud APIs. VPN concentrators only terminate remote-access tunnels. Signature-based endpoint AV focuses on file-based malware and does not govern cloud-application usage or data flows.

questions.q: A SOC lead is describing the primary function of a SIEM to a new analyst. Which statement best describes what a SIEM does?
choices: It automatically executes multi-step incident-response playbooks with minimal human involvement.
It replaces the network firewall by inspecting every packet at line rate.
It provides antivirus signatures to endpoints across the fleet.
It ingests logs and telemetry from many sources, normalises them, and correlates events to detect and prioritise security incidents.
questions.explanation: A Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform's core job is to collect logs and telemetry from disparate sources, normalise and index them, and correlate events using rules or analytics to surface prioritised alerts for investigation. Playbook execution and automated response are the job of a SOAR platform, which often integrates with the SIEM. A SIEM does not replace a firewall or distribute AV signatures — those are entirely different control planes.

questions.q: The SOC has just noticed a burst of malicious PowerShell activity across dozens of endpoints. The team wants to trigger an automated workflow that isolates each affected host, opens a ticket, and enriches the IOCs with threat-intel lookups — without an analyst manually clicking through every step. Which capability is designed for this?
choices: SIEM correlation rules.
A network intrusion-prevention system (IPS) signature update.
SOAR playbooks.
A CASB DLP policy.
questions.explanation: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platforms run playbooks that chain together actions across security tools — isolating an endpoint via EDR, opening a ticket, querying threat intelligence, notifying the responder — with little or no human interaction. SIEM correlation only detects and alerts; it does not orchestrate response. IPS signatures block traffic patterns but do not run cross-tool workflows. CASB DLP policies govern SaaS data movement, not endpoint response.

questions.q: During an incident review, a manager asks the team to describe the attacker's techniques using a shared, industry-standard taxonomy so the report is consistent with peer organisations. Which framework is designed for this purpose?
choices: PCI-DSS.
MITRE ATT&CK.
ITIL 4.
The OSI reference model.
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK is a curated knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) with unique identifiers (for example T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter). SOC teams use it as a common vocabulary in detections, post-incident reports, and purple-team exercises. PCI-DSS is a payment-card compliance standard, not a TTP taxonomy. ITIL 4 is an IT-service-management framework. The OSI model describes networking layers, not attacker behaviour.
